name: Pashto
variety: Southwestern (Kandahar) Pashto, the conservative variety on which the spelling is based and which the eSpeak NG base voice follows; the other dialect groups are summarised in the notes
sources: Penzl, Herbert (1955). A Grammar of Pashto: A Descriptive Study of the Dialect of Kandahar, Afghanistan. Washington: American Council of Learned Societies.
MacKenzie, D. N. (1959). A standard Pashto. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 22.
MacKenzie, D. N. (1987). Pashto. In Comrie (ed.), The World's Major Languages. London: Croom Helm.
Bečka, Jiří (1969). A Study in Pashto Stress. Prague: Academia.
Henderson, Michael M. T. (1983). Four varieties of Pashto. Journal of the American Oriental Society 103(3).
Skjærvø, Prods O. (1989). Pashto. In Schmitt (ed.), Compendium Linguarum Iranicarum. Wiesbaden: Reichert.
Tegey, Habibullah and Robson, Barbara (1996). A Reference Grammar of Pashto. Washington: Center for Applied Linguistics.
Elfenbein, Josef (1997). Pashto phonology. In Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa, volume 2. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Robson, Barbara and Tegey, Habibullah (2009). Pashto. In Windfuhr (ed.), The Iranian Languages. London: Routledge.
David, Anne Boyle (2014). Descriptive Grammar of Pashto and its Dialects. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
contrasts: dental versus retroflex stops /t̪ d̪/ : /ʈ ɖ/, and retroflex nasal /ɳ/ and flap /ɽ/ beside /n/ and /r/
three places for sibilants in the southwest: dental-alveolar /s z/, palato-alveolar /ʃ ʒ/ and retroflex /ʂ ʐ/ (letters ښ and ږ)
dental affricates /ts dz/ (څ ځ) versus palato-alveolar /tʃ dʒ/ (چ ج)
/a/ versus /ə/ versus /ɑ/; /ə/ occurs stressed as well as unstressed
free stress that distinguishes words and grammatical forms
final vowels and diphthongs carry gender and number: /aj/ (ی), /əj/ (ۍ, ئ), /e/ (ې), /i/ (ي), /a/ and /ə/ (ه)
no aspiration contrast in stops, unlike the neighbouring Indo-Aryan languages
/q f ʔ/ belong to the learned pronunciation of loanwords; everyday speech has [k], [p] and zero
allophony: /ʂ ʐ/ are retroflex (apical post-alveolar) fricatives in the southwest only; other dialects have different sounds for the letters ښ and ږ (see notes)
/ɳ/ is a nasalised retroflex flap [ɽ̃]; it does not begin words
/ɽ/ is a retroflex flap, often with a lateral release
/r/ is an alveolar tap or short trill
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars, [ɳ] before retroflexes and [m] before labials
voiceless stops are unaspirated or only weakly aspirated
/x ɣ/ are velar, with uvular variants next to back vowels
/ɑ/ is long and back; /a/ is short and front, and in unstressed syllables is reduced toward [ə]
/h/ is weak and is often dropped
phonotactics: many word-initial clusters of two consonants, including ones with falling or level sonority: ʃpa 'night', xwla 'mouth', zɣam 'tolerance', lmar 'sun', wror 'brother', dzməka 'earth'; a few of three consonants (ndror 'husband's sister')
final clusters of up to two consonants
the short vowels /a ə/ are not written except word-finally (ه), so clusters and vowels cannot be told apart from the spelling alone

stress.rule: Stress can fall on any syllable and belongs to the word and to the inflected form: it separates otherwise identical words and the perfective from the imperfective aspect of verbs (stress on the first syllable or prefix in the perfective); as a tendency it falls on the last syllable when that syllable is heavy and otherwise on the penult.
stress.cues: intensity, pitch and duration; unstressed /a/ is reduced toward [ə]

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed /a/ tends to [ə]; other vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: Strong dynamic stress and reduction of unstressed /a/ point to stress-timed tendencies, but no instrumental rhythm study is cited here, so the class is left as mixed.

length.notes: /ɑ/ is inherently longer than /a/ and /ə/, and /i e o u/ are longer than /a ə/. Older descriptions (Penzl 1955, MacKenzie 1959) set up long and short i and u; the contrast is marginal and later descriptions work with seven vowel qualities. Gemination is not contrastive.

intonation.declarative: pitch peaks on the stressed syllables of the main words, final fall to low on the verb at the end of the sentence
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of the statement with a final rise; an initial particle (ɑjɑ) is optional
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main accent; the utterance ends with a fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase or clause
intonation.accent_shape: high or rising pitch on the stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Instrumental work on Pashto intonation is sparse; this follows the reference grammars.

problems: ښ and ږ (phonemes S. and Z.) use the same friction recordings as ʃ and ʒ (ufric/sh, vocw/zh); only the formant transitions differ, so the retroflex and palato-alveolar sibilants sound almost the same; the base table's retroflex fricatives s. and z. with their own recordings (sh_rfx, zh_rfx) are not used
the retroflex stops ʈ ɖ use the alveolar burst recording (ustop/t_), and the retroflex flap and nasal use the plain r and n formant files (r3/r_, n/n_); retroflexion rests on transition settings only

the voiced retroflex stop ɖ is built from the voiceless recording ustop/t_ with no voiced formant frame, and in the output signal it has no voiced closure or burst, only a short dip between the vowels; the retroflex flap ɽ comes out as a long continuant, several times as long as the plain tap, not as a flap
/t d/ are defined as alveolar and /p t k/ use the aspirated English recordings; Pashto has dental, unaspirated stops

unwritten short vowels are often missing in the word list: about one entry in six of ps_list (about 122000 entries) has a run of four or more consonants, with و and ی taken as [w] and [j] (تلویزیونی as t@l'wjzjwni:, ننګرهار as n@n'grha:r, قلم as 'q@lm, مڼه as 'mn.a)

the final letters of the ye series are not kept apart: the replace table of ps_rules turns ي into ی, final ی is read [iː] by rule, and list entries do the same, so the masculine ending /aj/ is not produced (سړی is [saɽaˈiː], لرګی ['lrgi:], خدای [χədaːˈiː])

schwa is declared 'unstressed' and given the shortest vowel length (130) in the phoneme table, although stressed /ə/ is common in Pashto; no stress rule is set for ps, so a word without a stress mark in the dictionary gets the general default (penultimate) placement
خ and غ are uvular [χ ʁ] (phonemes X and Q) rather than velar [x ɣ]
IPA output labels coda l and r as voiceless (l̥, r̥)
good: the full southwestern consonant set is present: retroflex ʈ ɖ ɳ ɽ, retroflex fricatives, and the affricates ts and dz distinct from tʃ and dʒ
a [a] and a: [ɑː] differ in quality and length, schwa is a separate vowel, and e, i, o, u exist in short and long versions
ر is a tap, not the English approximant

notes: Dialect groups by the pronunciation of five letters (MacKenzie 1959; Henderson 1983; Elfenbein 1997; David 2014). Southwest (Kandahar): ښ [ʂ], ږ [ʐ], څ [ts], ځ [dz], ژ [ʒ]. Southeast (Quetta): ښ [ʃ], ږ [ʒ], څ [ts], ځ [dz], ژ [ʒ]. Northwest (central Ghilzai): ښ [ç], ږ [ʝ], ځ [z], څ [s] or [ts], ژ [ʒ]. Northeast (Yusufzai, Peshawar): ښ [x], ږ [ɡ], څ [s], ځ [z], ژ [dʒ]. The spelling is the same everywhere. The voice is marked 'status immature'.
